shortened: Whoso worships God through the drops of the sea and the sands of the desert and the leaves of the trees and their fruits, while remaining heedless of this Cause - such a one is among the idolaters, for his deeds have veiled him from Him through Whom all things were established in the Book.

order.why: Consider the varied things in which a person may become immersed.
Keep the theological critique of claimed certainty with its internal omission.
Read the setting-star image as a challenge to seeking light from a fading source.
Consider the choice of pebbles over pearls and thistles over nourishment.
shortened: They seek after thorns and thistles - that is, vain imaginings and idle fancies - while turning away from the pearls of utterance, clinging instead to pebbles and date-stones.

order.why: Keep the source’s severe contrast of carrion and a heavenly table.
shortened: Say: We have abandoned vain imaginings unto you, and have taken what We were commanded in the Book of God, the All-Knowing, the All-Informed. Say: We have abandoned the carrion, inasmuch as the heavenly table hath been sent down from the heaven of the bounty of our Lord, the Mighty, the All-Praised.

order.why: Read the call to break imagined idols in its account of religious opposition.
Consider certainty and the rejection of imagined idols through the divine Books.
shortened: Take hold of the divine Books with the hand of certitude, and with a mighty arm shatter and cast down the idols of vain imaginings.

order.why: Keep the emphatic turning toward this Book in its revealed context.
shortened: The books of the learned profit you not, nor do your ancient tales. Cast them behind you and hold fast unto this Book.

order.why: Read the blessing of those who cast aside veils and fancies.
shortened: Those who follow vain imaginings are in doubt and hypocrisy. Blessed is the strong one who hath rent asunder the veils and cast behind him idle fancies.

order.why: Consider the dawning of assurance and the invitation to witness.
Retain the harsh rhetoric of this call for penetrating vision in the source’s voice.
Keep the personal explanation of a brief scholarly exposition.
shortened: For a long time this Wronged One has not been inclined towards scholarly investigation, nor is He now, for in the early years such learned matters were discussed as would suffice. Now this brief exposition that hath been set forth was solely out of consideration for you.

order.why: Read the value of a letter through the divine good pleasure it expresses.
Consider the contrasting responses to words, learning, and the divine breeze.
Turn the warning about veils of glory toward ongoing self-examination.
shortened: Say: O My loved ones, reflect deeply upon the veils of glory and ever keep them before your eyes, lest perchance the glorified veils of idle fancy prevent you from the Court of Oneness.

order.why: Read the prayer about ignorance of one’s own ignorance and words without meanings.
Consider seeking each essence in its appropriate source and fruit from its tree.
shortened: The lights of the highest heaven shine not beneath the earth, and the pure soul findeth not its dwelling in the layers of dust. The manifest light shineth from the highest horizon, and the brilliant lamp gloweth within the delicate glass. Therefore must every essence be sought in its mine, and every fruit be hoped for from its tree.

order.why: Hear the blessing on a family and those holding to loving-kindness.
shortened: The glory be upon thee and upon thy father and thine uncle and thy mother and thy two brothers and upon those who have cast aside vain imaginings and idle fancies, holding fast to the loving-kindness of the True One, the Knower of things unseen.

order.why: Close the linked readings with turning toward God and the promise of protection.
Finish with the supplied clarification that the criticism of empty learning does not exclude story writing and useful practical skills.

questions: What does the lamp image suggest about the difference between knowing religious language and realizing its purpose?
What kinds of benefit and fruit do these readings ask us to seek from learning, and how might these be recognized over time?
How can a devotional practice deepen sincerity, and how can the same practice become a display or a substitute for change?
How does Dhammapada 19–20 illuminate the gap between recitation and practice while retaining its Buddhist account of liberation?
How can the sharp historical critiques be read without turning them into new claims of superiority over other people?
What would help a learner remain open to evidence, correction, and the possibility that cherished knowledge has become a veil?

references.label: 1 · Dhammapada 19–20 · Recitation and practice
references.note: Read verses 19–20 in Thanissaro Bhikkhu’s translation. The comparison of recitation without practice to counting another’s cattle asks what it means to participate in the contemplative life. Compare this with the compilation’s tests of learning and worship, while keeping the Buddhist emphasis on relinquishing passion, aversion, delusion, and clinging in view.
